name: Knee pain: causes and when to get help
summary: Knee pain can often be treated at home, and NHS 111 is the route for a badly swollen knee or a hot, red knee with a high temperature.
keyPoints: The NHS knee pain page lists causes including sprains and strains, tendonitis, torn ligaments, tendons or meniscus, a dislocated kneecap, bursitis, gout and Osgood-Schlatter's disease.
The NHS says knee pain can often be treated at home by reducing weight on the knee, using an ice pack and taking painkillers such as paracetamol or ibuprofen.
Hampshire and Isle of Wight NHS guidance suggests seeing a GP if knee pain has not eased within a few weeks.
The NHS advises calling NHS 111 if the knee is badly swollen or has changed shape, or if there is a very high temperature with redness or heat around the knee, which can signal infection.

body.heading: What causes knee pain?
body.body: The NHS knee pain page lists causes including sprains and strains, tendonitis, torn ligaments, tendons or meniscus, a dislocated kneecap, bursitis, gout and Osgood-Schlatter's disease. The NHS knee pain page links sprains and strains to overstretching, overusing or twisting the knee, often during exercise. An NHS trust leaflet lists pain, stiffness after rest and swelling as symptoms of osteoarthritis. NHS inform says the exact cause of knee osteoarthritis is unclear, and risk factors include ageing, a previous knee injury, being overweight and family history. An NHS trust page says changes seen on an X-ray do not necessarily match how bad the symptoms are. NHS inform says strengthening the muscles around the knee helps manage osteoarthritis symptoms.

body.heading: What can ease it at home?
body.body: The NHS says knee pain can often be treated at home by reducing weight on the knee, using an ice pack and taking painkillers such as paracetamol or ibuprofen.

body.heading: When should knee pain be seen by a GP or physiotherapist?
body.body: Hampshire and Isle of Wight NHS guidance suggests seeing a GP if knee pain has not eased within a few weeks. The NHS says people may be able to refer themselves to community musculoskeletal (MSK) physiotherapy services without seeing a GP. An NHS trust leaflet describes physiotherapy as the mainstay of treatment for pain at the front of the knee. An NHS trust leaflet on hip and knee osteoarthritis describes regular exercise, over-the-counter pain relief and losing a small amount of body fat.

body.heading: Which signs need urgent help?
body.body: The NHS advises calling NHS 111 if the knee is badly swollen or has changed shape, or if there is a very high temperature with redness or heat around the knee, which can signal infection.
